All numbers, tables and figures below were produced by the analysis run named above and are stored with it.

Summary

Kidney cancer metabolome (Hakimi et al. 2016, 140 pairs), 280 samples was analysed with the Metabolomics workflow (version 1.0.0) on the LSMA Analysis Lab. To find which metabolites differ between 'tumour' and 'normal' (column 'tissue'), adjusting for patient. In summary, 405 metabolites passed the thresholds; the model reached Q2 = 0.898. 4 point(s) are flagged under Limitations and should be read before the results are used.

  • 405 metabolites passed the thresholds.
  • The model reached Q2 = 0.898.

Introduction

From a table of metabolite intensities or concentrations to quality control with pooled QC and blank samples, normalisation, exploration, differential abundance and a cross-validated PLS-DA model. Peak picking and metabolite identification from raw spectra are done before the data reaches this workflow. The data analysed here is of kind 'metabolite_table'.

Aim

To find which metabolites differ between 'tumour' and 'normal' (column 'tissue'), adjusting for patient.

Methods

Assembled from what each completed stage recorded. Check it against the parameter tables below before using it in a write-up.

Metabolite intensities were read from ccrcc_hakimi_metabolites.tsv: 577 metabolites in 280 study samples, 0 pooled QC samples and 0 blanks. Scale: raw intensities or concentrations; zeros were treated as not measured.

Of 280 uploaded samples, 280 took part in the comparison of 'tissue' (normal, tumour); 0 samples were excluded by the analyst for the reasons listed under Data input.

Quality control: metabolites were kept when measured in at least 50% of the samples of at least one group of 'tissue', leaving 500 of 577.

Normalisation: probabilistic quotient normalisation: each sample is divided by the median of its ratios to a reference profile (the median of all study samples). Missing values (15% of the table): half of the smallest value measured for that metabolite (for values below the detection limit). Intensities were log2-transformed.

Differential abundance was tested with limma (empirical Bayes moderated t-test) on log2 intensities using the design ~ patient + tissue for the contrast tumour vs normal. P-values were adjusted with the BH method; metabolites with adjusted p-value below 0.05 and an absolute log2 fold change of at least 0 were called.

A multivariate model was fitted with OPLS-DA (ropls), pareto scaling, 7-fold cross-validation, 200 permutations: R2Y = 0.925, Q2 = 0.898, permutation p-value for Q2 = 0.005.

Random seed: 42. Software: R 4.5.2; Bioconductor 3.21; data.table 1.18.6.1; jsonlite 2.0.0; limma 3.64.3; ropls 1.40.0.

Analyses were run on the LSMA Analysis Lab (workflow 'metabolomics' version 1.0.0).

Stage 1 of 6

Data input Exploratory

Metabolomics measures the small molecules of a sample: sugars, amino acids, lipids, organic acids. A mass spectrometer (usually after liquid or gas chromatography) or an NMR instrument produces a signal for each of them, and software turns the raw spectra into a table with one number per metabolite and sample. This stage reads that table whichever way round it is laid out, treats a zero as "not measured", and sorts the samples into study samples, pooled quality-control (QC) samples and blanks.

Note. No pooled QC samples were recognised. The reproducibility of each metabolite over the run cannot be checked.

Sample preparation

Comparison: tissue, groups normal, tumour (reference: normal). Paired by patient. Adjusted for: patient. These choices were made before the analysis and the uploaded files were not changed.

No sample was excluded by the analyst.

Stage 2 of 6

Quality control and filtering Exploratory

Three filters are applied to the metabolites. Those missing in most samples of every group are removed. If pooled QC samples exist, the relative standard deviation (RSD: standard deviation divided by the mean) of each metabolite across them is computed, and metabolites above the limit are removed. If blanks exist, metabolites that are not clearly stronger in the samples than in the blanks are removed. A PCA with the QC samples and a plot of signal against run order show whether the instrument was stable.

Note. Flagged sample(s) with very low total signal: DIAG-16200, DIAG-16334, DIAG-16344.
Note. Fewer than three pooled QC samples: metabolites could not be filtered by reproducibility. Results for single metabolites deserve more caution.

Stage 3 of 6

Normalisation and missing values Exploratory

Each sample is divided by a factor that reflects how concentrated it was. With probabilistic quotient normalisation the factor is the median ratio of the sample's metabolites to a reference profile, so a few metabolites that really change do not distort it. Missing values are then filled in and the intensities are put on the log2 scale. The QC and blank samples are set aside from here on.

Note. Normalisation factors differ 9.5-fold between samples. Samples that needed a very large correction were much more dilute; their weak metabolites are less reliable.

How to interpret this stage

A metabolite is called when its adjusted p-value is below the threshold. Look at the size of the change too. In the demonstration data (urine of men against women), testosterone glucuronide and other steroid conjugates are much higher in men, as expected. Compare the result with and without adjustment for age and body mass index to see what a confounder does.

Stage 6 of 6

PLS-DA model Statistically supported

Partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) looks for the combination of metabolites that best separates two groups. The orthogonal variant (OPLS-DA) puts the group difference on one component and the unrelated variation on others. The model is judged by three numbers: R2Y, how well it fits the samples it was built on; Q2, how well it predicts samples that were held out in cross-validation; and the p-value of a permutation test, in which the group labels are shuffled and the whole procedure is repeated.

What this stage found

This stage recorded number of samples: 280, number of metabolites: 500, predictive components: 1, orthogonal components: 2, r2x: 0.372 and r2y: 0.925.

This is shown in Figure 14, Figure 15 and Figure 16.

How to interpret this stage

Read Q2 and the permutation p-value first. A Q2 above about 0.5 with a permutation p-value below 0.05 is a model that predicts; a high R2Y with a low Q2 is overfitting. If no model can be built, the groups cannot be told apart from these metabolites, and that is the result. Then use the VIP list together with the differential abundance table: metabolites high in both are the ones to follow up.
